    4. -algebras, measures, and their properties#

    The preceding discussion of outer measure provides a size for every subset of , but the Vitali counterexample shows that no countably additive, translation-invariant extension of interval length can be defined on every subset of . To obtain additivity, we must restrict the domain of a measure from to a carefully chosen collection of sets.

    That collection must still support the standard operations consistens with measure properties: complements, countable unions, and therefore countable intersections. -algebras supply exactly this structure. Once the domain is in place, countable additivity yields the basic inequalities and continuity properties that make measures useful in later integration theory.

    After studying these notes, you will be able to do the following.

    • Distinguish rings, algebras, and -algebras and use their closure properties.

    • Generate a -algebra and identify standard Borel generating families.

    • Verify that a set function is a measure and derive its basic inequalities.

    • Relate additivity, finite superadditivity, and monotone continuity.

    • Compute measures of monotone limits of sets and recognize why the finite-measure hypothesis in continuity from above is necessary.

    4.1 Algebras, sigma-algebras, and generators#

    The domain of a measure must be stable under the operations used in countable decompositions. Rings and algebras isolate the finite operations; -algebras add countable unions.

    A slightly more involved example is that of a -algebra generated by a partition.

    More in general, given any collection of sets we define the generated -algebra as the “minimal” -sigma algebra containing those sets. Such a notion is valid because of the following property.

    Proof of Proposition 4.4#

    Thanks to the property above, we can define the minimal -algebra of a set that satisfies given properties. Indeed, one just takes the intersection of all -algebras of satisying that property. The resulting object is a -algebra by the property above and is clearly not larger than any other -algebra satisfying the properties in question (in virtue of being the intersection).

    Generated -algebras are usually handled through this minimality property. For example, to compare two generating families, it suffices to show that each member of one family belongs to the -algebra generated by the other. An explicit list of all elements of is, on the other hand, very difficult to provide.

    4.2 Measures and their basic properties#

    A measure assigns a nonnegative extended real number to every set in a -algebra.

    Countable additivity and nonnegativity ensure that every measure is monotone and countably subadditive. Consequently, on its -algebra, a measure satisfies all defining properties of an outer measure.
